values: Materials and setup｜S1—S4 are all editorially fictional

Using only the fictional records below, the research question is “how do the proportions willing to take part in the activity differ between the two groups in the given sample?” Do not recruit real people, collect personal information, evaluate real groups or study activity effects.

S1｜7 input rows, with fields ID, group, willing to take part (yes/no/missing): 01/A/yes; 02/A/no; 03/A/missing; 04/B/yes; 05/B/yes; 06/B/no; row 7 is 03/A/missing, completely identical to row 3. All IDs and groups are fictional, and A and B are not any real population category.

S2｜Delete rows completely duplicated on ID and all fields, keeping the first record. Missing values must not be filled in as “no” or “yes”. This item provides no sampling, random assignment, weighting, pre-post measurement or activity participation effect materials, and none may be added.

S3｜Each group's willingness proportion = number of “yes” answers / that group's valid (yes or no) answers; the overall proportion uses all valid answers as the denominator. The missing rate = missing people after de-duplication / total people after de-duplication. Write only B minus A as a percentage point difference, keep all proportions to 1 decimal place, and make no significance or causal judgment.

S4｜Submit four work products: the cleaning log (7→6), the denominator and missing value table, the A/B and overall proportion calculation table, and a 100—150 character statement of result limitations. Keep an independent first draft before checking the answers, and explain that valid answers are not the whole sample and that the two groups are not random, so no population or effect can be inferred.

Review requirements｜The missing value for 03 cannot be treated as no, and a complete duplicate is deleted only once; the group proportions use 2 and 3 as denominators, the overall uses 5, and the missing rate uses 6. A small-sample difference is not an activity effect.
Tasks and outputs

Clean the 7 rows according to S2 and list each group's total, valid count, missing count and “yes” count, calculating each formula according to S3. Write the group difference and limitations, and do not interpret the motives of fictional members.

Submit the four work products plus the independent first draft and revisions. The result statement applies only to the given records; with no representativeness, random assignment or pre-post measurement, it cannot explain real social trends or causal activity effects.
Reference answers (finish independently first, then check)

After deleting row 7, which completely duplicates 03, 6 people remain. A has a total of 3, 2 valid, 1 missing and 1 “yes”; B has a total of 3, 3 valid, 0 missing and 2 “yes”. Overall there is a total of 6, 5 valid, 1 missing and 3 “yes”.

A's willingness proportion is 1/2 = 50.0%; B is 2/3 = 66.7%; the overall is 3/5 = 60.0%; the missing rate is 1/6 = 16.7%. B minus A = 16.7 percentage points (calculated from unrounded proportions first, then rounded to 1 decimal place). This is not a 16.7% relative increase.

Example conclusion: in the given fictional sample, the willingness proportion among B's valid answers is 16.7 percentage points higher than A's; A has 1 missing value and both groups are very small. No sampling, random assignment, weighting or pre-post measurement is provided, so real population willingness, individual motives or activity effects cannot be inferred. Denominators, missing values and method limitations should be reported together.
Boundaries and review

All materials are fictional, with no real personal materials, weights or causal design. This item is a descriptive calculation only; real research additionally requires material sources, ethics review, consent and appropriate methods, and the work grants no independent research or psychological service authority.

description.text: Social scientists who study social groups, institutions and interpersonal interaction, design surveys or interviews, analyze materials and interpret research results. Research questions, sampling and measurement determine the boundaries of conclusions; this is not diagnosing people from observation. This page uses a fictional questionnaire to practice de-duplication, missing value handling and proportion interpretation, and real research requires separate ethics review and data authority.
